By the third week of August, the reservoir had dropped forty feet, and the town began to remember itself.

It happened slowly at first, marked by pale bands of bleached silt along the granite bluffs—mineral rings showing where the water used to hold the weight of the sky. Then came the stumps of the drowned orchard, black and slick as whalebone, poking through the shallows near the northern cove. By the time the first slate tiles of the church roof breached the surface, the county road was already lined with parked cars. People came with long lenses and folding chairs, leaning against the rusted guardrails to stare down at what the drought had given back.

Julian watched them from his porch on the upper ridge, a cup of lukewarm coffee cooling in his hands. He did not go down to the shoreline during the day. He did not want to hear strangers narrating the geography of a place they had never walked, pointing at the wet stones and calling them quaint, or eerie, or sad.

He had been seven years old in the autumn of 1974, when the valley was cleared for the dam. Seven is a strange age to lose a home: old enough to carry the exact floor plan of a bedroom in your bones, young enough that every street feels endless and every hill looks like a mountain. He remembered the smell of wet wool in the school cloakroom, the loose flagstone outside the post office that clicked like a knuckle whenever you stepped on it, and the way the river sounded in April, thick and loud with snowmelt. Mostly, he remembered the silence of the last week, when the furniture trucks had gone and the windows stood open to the wind, curtains already pulled down.

On a Tuesday morning, when the air still held the blue chill of four o’clock, Julian walked down to the dock. The planks were dry and splintered; the water had retreated so far that the pilings stood naked in the mud, crusted with dead zebra mussels. He dragged his old cedar skiff twenty yards across the cracked lakebed until the hull floated, climbed in, and fitted the oars into the locks.

Mist hung low over the reservoir, swallowing the far shore and turning the water into a sheet of brushed pewter. Without the tourists, without the hum of traffic on the highway above, the valley was quiet enough to hear the drip of water falling from his oar blades.

He rowed toward the center, guided by an old, internal compass. Here was the bend where the bridge used to cross. Beneath the murky green surface, he could just make out the dark geometry of stone walls, softened by decades of algae. A school of perch darted out from what had once been the cellar of the hardware store, vanishing into the gloom.

Ten minutes later, the steeple loomed out of the fog.

It was smaller than it had any right to be. In Julian’s memory, the bell tower of St. Jude’s had been a towering thing, a needle stitched into the clouds. Now, jutting from the flat water, the limestone looked stubby and tired. The heavy bronze bell had been removed before the flooding—hauled away on a flatbed truck to a parish two counties east—leaving the belfry empty, just four arched openings framing the white mist.

Julian shipped the oars and let the skiff drift until the bow bumped gently against the masonry. He reached out and laid his bare palm against the stone.

It was cold, slick with riverweed, and smelled intensely of mud and iron. Above the waterline, where the August sun had baked the exposed stone for a fortnight, the algae had already dried into a brittle, chalky crust that flaked off under his thumb.

He waited for something to happen. He had lived on the rim of this valley for thirty years, half-believing that if the water ever went away, some locked drawer inside him would finally spring open. He expected grief, or a sudden, overwhelming rush of the boy he had been.

Instead, there was only the quiet slap of water against the cedar hull, and a strange, gentle embarrassment—as if he had walked uninvited into a room where someone was sleeping.

Looking down through the clear shallows around the foundation, he saw a rusted bicycle wheel half-buried in silt, a porcelain insulator from a telephone pole, the stub of a granite doorstep. Everything looked impossibly narrow. The grand square where he had learned to ride a bicycle was just a cramped patch of mud. The air didn’t suit these ruins. Under fifty feet of dark water, the town had been preserved in a kind of amber, magnified by refraction and memory into something mythic. Out here in the dry heat, exposed to sunlight and camera shutters, it was merely rotting. The timber frames would warp and split; the mortar would crumble into sand.

Water hadn’t destroyed Aldermere, he realized. Water had kept it.

A cool breath of wind moved across the reservoir, shredding the mist into pale ribbons. Julian looked up. Beyond the western ridge, where the sky had been glaring and cloudless for two solid months, a low bank of bruised gray clouds was slowly pushing over the pines. The air smelled faintly of ozone—the metallic promise of a changing season.

Julian pushed off from the limestone wall, watching the ripples widen until they blurred the reflection of the empty belfry. He settled the oars back into the locks and turned the bow toward the high shore, pulling steady, unhurried strokes. Behind him, the drowned town faded back into the fog. He hoped the rain came hard, and he hoped it stayed for weeks.
